passages.title: The Camel
passages.text: The camel lives in the desert. It walks on hot sand. Its feet are wide and soft. They do not sink. A camel has a hump on its back. The hump holds fat. The fat helps it live with no food. A camel can drink a lot of water at one time. Then it can go for days with no drink. It has long lashes. They keep sand out of its eyes. People have used camels for a long time.

questions.stem: What does a camel's hump hold?
options: Fat
Water
Sand
Milk

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Camels like to sleep in the cold snow.
A camel's body helps it live in the desert.
People use sand to make soft feet.
Camels need to drink water every single hour.

questions.stem: The text says the camel's feet do not sink. What does sink mean?
options: get very hot in the sun
walk fast
go down into something
turn to one side

passages.title: Bees at Work
passages.text: Bees live in a hive. Many bees live in one hive. Each bee has a job. Some bees make wax. Some bees keep the hive clean. Some bees fly out to find flowers. They drink sweet juice from the flowers. Then they fly back home. In the hive, the juice turns into honey. The bees eat the honey in the cold months. People like honey too. It is sweet and good.

questions.stem: Where do bees find the sweet juice?
options: In the wax
In the rain
In tree roots
In flowers

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Bees work together to make honey.
Bees are afraid of the cold winter months.
People make the wax for bees.
Flowers grow best in a hive.

questions.stem: Why do bees need honey in the cold months?
options: The hive is too clean to live in.
There are few flowers to visit then.
They want to give all of the honey to people.
The wax is too hot for them to eat.

passages.title: Brush Your Teeth
passages.text: Your teeth help you eat. You need to take care of them. Brush your teeth two times a day. Brush when you get up. Brush at night too. Use a soft brush and a bit of paste. Brush for two full minutes. Do not skip the back teeth. Sweet food can hurt your teeth. Drink water, not soda. Then go to see a dentist each year. A dentist checks that your teeth are strong.

questions.stem: How long should you brush your teeth?
options: For two hours
For ten seconds
For two minutes
For half an hour

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Why soda tastes so much sweeter than water
How a dentist got the job
Where to buy a soft brush
How to keep your teeth healthy

questions.stem: The text says, Do not skip the back teeth. What does skip mean?
options: leave out
brush hard
look at
pull out

passages.title: The Moon at Night
passages.text: At night, you can often see the moon in the sky. The moon does not make its own light. It shines because light from the sun hits it. The moon moves around the Earth. One trip takes about a month. As it moves, we see more or less of its bright side. That is why the moon seems to change shape. Some nights it looks round and full. On other nights it looks like a thin curve. The moon has no air or water, so no plants or animals live there.

questions.stem: How long does the moon take to go around the Earth?
options: About one day
About one month
About one week
About one year

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: The moon is a good place for plants and trees to grow.
The sun moves around the moon each night of the year.
The moon shines with sun light and seems to change shape.
People can only see the moon during the cold winter months.

questions.stem: Why could a person not live on the moon without help?
options: It is too close to the sun.
It is dark there all the time.
It is made of bright light.
There is no air to breathe.

passages.title: Fast Falcons
passages.text: The falcon is a fast bird. It has sharp eyes. It can see a mouse from far away. When it spots food, it folds its wings and dives. Some can dive faster than a car. People in Saudi Arabia have trained falcons for a long time. A trainer works with the bird each day. The bird learns to fly back to its trainer. The trainer wears a thick glove. The glove keeps the trainer safe from sharp claws.

questions.stem: What does the trainer wear?
options: A thick glove
A bright hat
A long, heavy coat
A soft shoe

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Cars can go faster than any kind of bird.
Falcons are fast hunters that people train.
Small animals hide from the hot sun all day.
Gloves are made from strong and thick cloth.

questions.stem: The text says, When it spots food, it folds its wings. What does spots mean?
options: paints
drops
sees
hides

passages.title: Drink Your Water
passages.text: Your body needs water every day. More than half of your body is water. You lose water when you sweat and breathe. You need to drink to put it back. If you do not drink enough, you may feel tired. You may get a headache too. Hot days make you sweat more. So drink more on hot days. Take a bottle of water with you to school. Melons and oranges have a lot of water in them. They help you feel good all day.

questions.stem: Which food does the text say has water in it?
options: White rice
Bread
Nuts
Oranges

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Drinking water keeps your body healthy.
Hot days are the best days for sports.
Melons are the best fruit to grow.
Schools should sell more water bottles.

questions.stem: On a hot day, Lina feels tired and has a headache. What might help her most?
options: Running in the sun
Drinking some water
Eating salty chips
Skipping her lunch

passages.title: Water on the Move
passages.text: The water on Earth is always moving. When the sun warms a lake or the sea, some water turns into a gas. This gas rises into the sky. High up, the air is cool. The gas cools and turns back into tiny drops. Many drops gather to form clouds. When the drops grow heavy, they fall as rain or snow. The rain fills rivers, lakes, and the sea. Then the sun warms the water again, and the cycle starts over. The same water has moved this way for millions of years.

questions.stem: What makes the gas turn back into drops?
options: Heavy rain on a big lake
Warm sand next to the sea
Cool air high in the sky
Bright light from the moon

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Clouds are made of small bits of dust and sand.
Rivers are always much bigger than lakes.
Snow falls only in very cold countries.
Water moves in a cycle between Earth and sky.

questions.stem: The text says, Many drops gather to form clouds. What does gather mean?
options: come together
fall down
dry up
break apart

passages.title: How Do We See?
passages.text: Long ago, a scientist named Ibn al-Haytham lived in Cairo. He was born in Basra about one thousand years ago. He wanted to know how we see. Many people then thought that light came out of our eyes. Ibn al-Haytham tested this idea. He studied light in a dark room. The room had a small hole in one wall. Light came in through the hole. It made a picture on the far wall. He showed that light comes into our eyes from the things around us. He wrote a famous book about light.

questions.stem: Where did Ibn al-Haytham study light?
options: On a boat out in the open sea
In a dark room with a small hole
In a garden full of bright sun
At the top of a very tall tower

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Cairo was the biggest city in the old world.
Many people long ago had very weak eyes.
Ibn al-Haytham tested ideas to learn how we see.
Light can only travel through a room that is dark.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Ibn al-Haytham from the text?
options: He did not like to read books or write them.
He thought that light came out of our eyes.
He spent his whole life in the city where he was born.
He checked ideas instead of just believing them.

passages.title: Playing as a Team
passages.text: Football is one of the most popular sports in the world. A team has eleven players on the field. One player is the goalkeeper. Only this player may touch the ball with the hands. Even then, it must be near the goal. The rest use their feet, heads, and chests. To score, a team must get the ball into the other team's goal. Good teams pass the ball to each other a lot. A player who shares the ball helps the whole team win.

questions.stem: How many players does a team have on the field?
options: Eleven
Nine
Twelve
Fifteen

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: The goalkeeper scores most of the goals in a game.
Football has rules and works best with teamwork.
Football is played in only a few countries.
Players should never use their heads.

questions.stem: The text says football is popular. What does popular mean?
options: very hard to learn
played only at night
liked by many people
new and not known

passages.title: The Date Palm
passages.text: The date palm is one of the oldest farm trees in the world. It grows well in hot, dry places like Saudi Arabia. A date palm can grow taller than a four-story building. Its long leaves are called fronds. Farmers climb the trees to pick the sweet, sticky fruit in late summer. Dates are full of energy, so travelers in the desert have carried them for thousands of years. People also used every part of the tree. They made baskets and mats from the fronds and built roofs from the trunks.

questions.stem: What are the long leaves of the date palm called?
options: Trunks
Roots
Seeds
Fronds

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: The date palm has long been useful to people in dry lands.
Farmers prefer to grow their trees in cold, wet places.
Dates are always picked early in the winter months.
Baskets are the most important thing that people make from trees.

questions.stem: What can you infer about the date palm?
options: It grows only in cold mountain areas.
It does not need much rain to grow.
It has no uses besides its sweet fruit.
It is a new kind of tree from farms.

passages.title: Mountains of Fire
passages.text: Deep under the ground, it is so hot that some rock melts. This melted rock is called magma. Sometimes magma pushes up through a crack in the Earth's crust. When it reaches the surface, it is called lava. A mountain that forms this way is a volcano. Some volcanoes erupt with a loud blast of ash and gas. Others let lava flow out slowly like thick syrup. Saudi Arabia has large fields of old lava called harrats. Scientists watch volcanoes closely. They measure small shakes in the ground to warn people early.

questions.stem: What is magma called when it reaches the surface?
options: Ash
Crust
Lava
Syrup

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Scientists cannot learn anything at all about volcanoes.
All volcanoes explode with a loud blast of ash.
Lava is the coldest kind of rock on the Earth.
Volcanoes form when melted rock rises to the surface.

questions.stem: The text says some volcanoes erupt with a loud blast. What does erupt mean?
options: burst out suddenly
cool down slowly
sink into the sea
grow new plants

passages.title: Why We Need Sleep
passages.text: Sleep is not wasted time. While you sleep, your body is busy. It repairs muscles and helps you grow. Your brain sorts what you learned during the day and stores it as memories. Children your age need about nine to twelve hours of sleep each night. Without enough sleep, it is hard to pay attention in class. You may also feel grumpy. To sleep well, go to bed at the same time each night. Turn off screens an hour before bed, because their bright light can keep your brain awake.

questions.stem: How much sleep do children your age need each night?
options: About four to five hours
About nine to twelve hours
About six to seven hours
About fifteen to sixteen hours

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Screens help children fall asleep much faster.
Muscles grow only when people exercise.
Sleep helps the body and brain stay healthy.
Going to bed very late is a good habit.

questions.stem: Omar watched videos late and slept only six hours. What will most likely happen at school?
options: He will remember more than usual.
He will feel full of energy all day.
He will grow much taller that day.
He may find it hard to focus.

passages.title: Return of the Oryx
passages.text: The Arabian oryx is a white antelope with long, straight horns. It lives in the deserts of Arabia, where it can go for weeks without drinking. It gets water from the plants it eats and from the morning dew. Its pale coat reflects sunlight and helps it stay cool. Sadly, hunting wiped out the wild oryx by the early 1970s. A few animals still lived in zoos, however. Scientists bred them with care and later released small herds into protected areas. Today, more than a thousand oryx live in the wild again. The animal has become a symbol of how people can save a species.

questions.stem: Where does the oryx get water when it is not drinking?
options: From plants and morning dew
From deep holes that it digs
From snow on the mountains
From streams in the forest

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: The oryx has always lived in very large numbers in zoos.
People helped the oryx return after it disappeared from the wild.
Hunting is the best way to keep desert animals safe.
The oryx needs to drink water every single day in order to stay alive.

questions.stem: The text says scientists released small herds into protected areas. What does released mean?
options: counted
fed
set free
caught

passages.title: The Bicycle Changes Shape
passages.text: The first bicycles, built in the early 1800s, had no pedals. Riders pushed against the ground with their feet, like on a scooter. Later, inventors added pedals to the front wheel. To go faster, they made that front wheel huge, sometimes taller than a man. These high-wheel bikes were fast but dangerous, because riders could easily fall forward. In the 1880s, the safety bicycle solved this problem. It had two wheels of the same size and a chain that turned the back wheel. Its design worked so well that most bikes today still look much the same.

questions.stem: How did riders move the very first bicycles?
options: By turning pedals on the big back wheel
By pulling a long chain with their hands
By using a small engine under the seat
By pushing on the ground with their feet

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: The bicycle changed over time to become safer to ride.
High-wheel bikes were the safest bikes ever made.
Scooters were invented before cars and trains.
Bicycles today look nothing like the safety bicycle of the 1880s.

questions.stem: The text says the safety bicycle's design worked well. What does design mean?
options: the price it cost
the way it was made
the name it was given
the speed it reached

passages.title: Reefs of the Red Sea
passages.text: The Red Sea is home to some of the most colorful coral reefs on Earth. Coral may look like rock or plants. But it is made of tiny animals called polyps. Each polyp builds a hard skeleton around itself. Over many years, millions of these skeletons pile up and form a reef. Reefs give food and shelter to fish, turtles, and many other sea animals. Red Sea corals are special. They can handle warmer water than most corals can. Scientists study them to learn how other reefs might survive as the oceans get warmer.

questions.stem: What are coral reefs made of?
options: Pieces of broken sea glass
Rocks pushed up by volcanoes
The skeletons of tiny animals
Plants that grow on the sand

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Coral reefs are made of plants that grow on rocks.
Turtles and fish build reefs so they can stay out of the hot sun.
Most of the world's oceans are getting much colder.
Red Sea reefs are living homes that scientists study.

questions.stem: Why might Red Sea corals be important for the future?
options: They may show how reefs can live in warmer seas.
They may be used to build new houses on the coast.
They may stop the fish from eating sea plants.
They may make the water in other seas much cooler.

passages.title: Power from the Sun
passages.text: The sun sends far more energy to Earth than people could ever use. Solar panels capture some of this energy and turn it into electricity. Each panel holds many cells, which are usually made from a material called silicon. When sunlight hits these cells, it knocks tiny particles called electrons loose. As the electrons move, they make an electric current. Saudi Arabia gets strong sunshine for most of the year, so it is a great place for solar power. The country is building large solar farms in the desert. One problem is dust, which can cover the panels and lower how much power they make.

questions.stem: What material are solar cells usually made from?
options: Copper
Silicon
Iron
Rubber

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Dust is the main source of energy for machines in the desert.
Electricity can only be made by burning oil.
Solar panels change sunlight into useful electricity.
Silicon is found only in the deserts of Arabia.

questions.stem: Why might workers clean solar panels often in the desert?
options: So the panels change their color
So the sun shines for longer hours
So the cells turn back into sand
So dust does not lower their power

passages.title: The Elephant Clock
passages.text: About eight hundred years ago, an engineer named Al-Jazari worked in the city of Diyarbakir. He designed dozens of clever machines, such as water clocks, pumps, and devices that moved by themselves. One of his most famous inventions was the elephant clock. It used flowing water to keep track of time. Every half hour, a small figure struck a cymbal and a bird whistled. Al-Jazari also wrote a long book with drawings. The book explained exactly how to build each machine. Because he kept such a careful record, engineers today have been able to rebuild several of his inventions and see how they work.

questions.stem: What did the elephant clock use to measure time?
options: Flowing water
Burning candles
Falling sand
Moving shadows

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Elephants were used to carry heavy machines across the city.
Al-Jazari invented clever machines and recorded how to build them.
Modern engineers have never been able to rebuild old machines.
Al-Jazari mostly wrote poems and stories about the famous birds of his city.

questions.stem: The text says Al-Jazari designed pumps and devices. What does devices mean?
options: drawings or maps
cities or towns
machines or tools
songs or poems

passages.title: Why We Exercise
passages.text: Doctors say that children should be active for at least sixty minutes every day. Exercise makes the heart stronger. The heart is a muscle that pumps blood through the body. A stronger heart can send more oxygen to the muscles and brain with each beat. Running, swimming, and playing football also build strong bones and help children keep a healthy weight. Exercise helps the mind as well. Many students find that they feel calmer and can concentrate better after active play. You do not need special equipment to stay active. Walking, jumping rope, or helping with chores at home all count.

questions.stem: How long should children be active each day?
options: At least ten minutes
Exactly three hours
About twenty minutes
At least sixty minutes

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Regular exercise helps both the body and the mind.
Children need special equipment before they can exercise.
The heart is the only muscle that gets stronger.
Chores at home are more tiring than playing football.

questions.stem: Which student is most likely following the doctors' advice?
options: Ali, who plays video games all afternoon
Sara, who plays outside for an hour daily
Huda, who runs only once or twice a month
Fahad, who reads in his room every evening

passages.title: Forests in the Sea
passages.text: Along parts of the Saudi coast on the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf grow unusual trees called mangroves. Most trees would die if their roots were soaked in salt water, but mangroves have adapted to survive there. Some of their roots grow upward out of the mud like small pencils, allowing the trees to breathe when the tide is high. Their leaves can also get rid of extra salt. Mangrove forests protect coastlines by slowing waves and holding soil in place during storms. Their tangled roots create safe nurseries where young fish and shrimp can hide from larger predators. For these reasons, Saudi Arabia has planted millions of new mangrove trees in recent years.

questions.stem: How do some mangrove roots help the tree breathe?
options: They spread deep under the sand.
They wrap tightly around rocks.
They grow upward out of the mud.
They float on top of the waves.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Mangroves are trees that grow best in cold, snowy mountains.
Fish and shrimp plant mangrove trees along the shore.
Storms are the main reason that coastlines exist at all.
Mangroves are adapted to salty coasts and help protect them.

questions.stem: The text says mangroves have adapted to survive in salt water. What does adapted mean?
options: changed to fit where they live
moved quickly to a new place
grown taller than other trees
stopped growing for a long time

passages.title: Books for Everyone
passages.text: Before the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand. This was slow work, and a single book could take months to finish. Printers in China and Korea had already used movable type. But around 1450, a German metalworker named Johannes Gutenberg built a press with movable metal letters. Workers arranged the letters to form a page, covered them with ink, and pressed paper against them. Then the same letters could be moved around to make the next page. Suddenly, hundreds of copies of a book could be made in the time it once took to make one. As books became cheaper, more people learned to read, and new ideas spread faster than ever before.

questions.stem: What did Gutenberg's press use to print pages?
options: Carved wooden boards
Movable metal letters
Hand-painted pictures
Long rolls of cloth

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Copying books by hand was faster than using a machine.
Gutenberg was the first person to write books in German.
The printing press made books faster and cheaper to produce.
Few people wanted to read after the printing press appeared.

questions.stem: What can you infer about books in Europe before the printing press?
options: Most families had large home libraries.
They were all written in the German language.
They were shorter than books are today.
Few people could afford to own them.

passages.title: The Rock Tombs of Hegra
passages.text: In the northwest of Saudi Arabia lies Hegra, an ancient city near AlUla. About two thousand years ago, it was an important stop for traders who carried goods such as incense and spices. The Nabataeans, the people who built the city, carved more than one hundred grand tombs straight into the sandstone cliffs. Some of the carved fronts are several stories high, and they still show fine decorations and writing. The dry desert air has helped protect them for centuries. In 2008, Hegra became the first place in Saudi Arabia to be named a World Heritage Site. Today, visitors from around the world come to admire how skillfully its builders shaped solid rock.

questions.stem: What did the Nabataeans carve into the cliffs?
options: Grand tombs
Market stalls
Long roads
Water wells

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Hegra is a new city that was built for modern tourists.
Hegra is an ancient city known for tombs carved into rock.
Traders today still carry incense through AlUla on the backs of camels.
Sandstone is too soft for anything to be carved into it.

questions.stem: The text says visitors come to admire the builders' work. What does admire mean?
options: try to copy exactly
complain about
look at with respect
take apart slowly

passages.title: The Wisdom of Ants
passages.text: Although a single ant has a tiny brain, an ant colony can solve surprisingly hard problems. When a worker ant finds food, it walks back to the nest and leaves behind a trail of chemicals called pheromones. Other ants detect this scent with their antennae and follow the trail to the food, adding more pheromones as they go. Ants on a shorter route finish the trip more quickly, so they lay down scent more often. As a result, the shortest trail soon becomes the strongest, and the colony settles on the most efficient path without any leader planning it. Computer scientists have studied this behavior. They have written programs, inspired by ants, that help plan delivery routes and guide traffic through communication networks.

questions.stem: How do ants detect pheromones?
options: With their eyes
With their legs
With their jaws
With their antennae

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Ant colonies use scent trails to find efficient paths.
Each ant in a colony has a very large and clever brain.
Computer programs taught ants how to find their food.
Ants always choose the longest path back to the nest.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about how a colony solves problems?
options: One leader ant gives orders to all the others.
Many simple actions add up to a smart result.
Each ant plans the whole route before leaving.
Ants learn the best routes by watching people.

passages.title: The Modern Olympics
passages.text: The first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens, Greece, in 1896. They were inspired by sports festivals held in ancient Greece more than two thousand years earlier. A French educator named Pierre de Coubertin believed that contests between countries could build friendship and understanding among nations. Only about fourteen countries sent athletes to those first Games, and all of the athletes were men. Today, more than two hundred nations participate, and the Games include dozens of sports, from swimming and gymnastics to newer events such as skateboarding. Women now compete in almost every sport as well. Saudi Arabia first competed in 1972. Since then, its athletes have won medals in several events, including show jumping on horseback, running, and karate.

questions.stem: Where were the first modern Olympic Games held?
options: Paris, France
Rome, Italy
Athens, Greece
London, England

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: The modern Olympics have always included more than two hundred nations.
Pierre de Coubertin was the first athlete to win an Olympic medal.
Skateboarding was one of the main sports at the first Games.
The modern Olympics grew from a small start into a global event.

questions.stem: The text says more than two hundred nations participate. What does participate mean?
options: take part
watch closely
pay money
stay away

passages.title: Fuel for the Morning
passages.text: Nutrition experts often describe breakfast as fuel for the morning. After a night without food, the body's supply of energy is low. The brain, in particular, depends on a steady flow of glucose, a sugar that comes from the food we eat. Without this fuel, many students find it hard to stay alert in class. Students who eat a balanced breakfast often find it easier to concentrate and to remember information during their lessons. A balanced meal combines several food groups: whole grains such as oats or bread, protein from eggs, beans, or yogurt, and a piece of fruit. Sugary cereals and pastries may give quick energy, but that energy fades fast. As a result, students who eat them often feel hungry and tired long before lunch.

questions.stem: According to the text, what does the brain depend on?
options: A large amount of salt
A steady flow of glucose
A long rest after lunch
Extra hours of sleep

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Sugary cereals are the best choice for a school morning.
Students should skip breakfast and eat a much larger lunch at school instead.
A balanced breakfast gives students lasting energy for learning.
Eggs and beans are the only foods that contain protein.

questions.stem: Why might a student who eats only a sweet pastry feel hungry by mid-morning?
options: It has too much protein in it.
It is full of whole grains.
It makes the heart beat slower.
Its quick energy fades fast.

passages.title: Dunes on the Move
passages.text: The Rub' al Khali, or Empty Quarter, stretches across southern Saudi Arabia and several neighboring countries, and it contains one of the largest continuous areas of sand on Earth. Its dunes are not fixed parts of the landscape. Instead, they migrate gradually as the wind carries grains of sand up the gentle slope on one side and lets them tumble down the steeper face on the other. Depending on the strength and direction of the main winds, a dune may advance several meters in a single year. Some dunes in the Empty Quarter rise more than two hundred meters, which is taller than most buildings in a typical city. Engineers who build roads and railways across deserts must therefore expect the sand to move, and they design fences and barriers to keep it from burying their work.

questions.stem: How tall can some dunes in the Empty Quarter be?
options: More than two hundred meters
About twenty meters
Less than five meters
Nearly two thousand meters

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: The Empty Quarter is a small desert that is found only inside Saudi Arabia.
Desert dunes move with the wind, which affects how people build.
Dunes stay in the same place for thousands of years at a time.
Skyscrapers are built in the desert to block the strong winds.

questions.stem: The text says the dunes migrate gradually. What does migrate most nearly mean?
options: grow larger every year
disappear completely
move from place to place
become hard as rock

passages.title: A Lucky Mistake
passages.text: In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a vacation and found that mold had grown on one of his dishes of bacteria. Rather than throwing the dish away, he examined it carefully and noticed that the bacteria around the mold had been destroyed. Fleming identified the substance that the mold produced and named it penicillin. However, more than ten years passed before other researchers, including Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, found ways to make penicillin in large amounts. By the 1940s, this first widely used antibiotic was saving countless lives by treating infections that had often been deadly. Today, doctors warn that antibiotics must be used wisely. When these medicines are overused, bacteria can change over time so that the drugs no longer work against them.

questions.stem: What did Fleming notice about the bacteria near the mold?
options: They had grown much larger.
They had changed color.
They had turned into mold.
They had been destroyed.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the text?
options: A careful observation led to penicillin, an important medicine.
Fleming made large amounts of penicillin entirely by himself in his own lab.
Mold is always harmful and should be thrown away at once.
Antibiotics should be used as often as possible by everyone.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about Fleming's discovery?
options: He had planned to grow mold on the dish all along.
Noticing an accident closely can lead to progress.
He produced large amounts of penicillin by himself.
Antibiotics work best when people use them often.

passages.title: The Father of Algebra
passages.text: During the ninth century, Baghdad became one of the world's leading centers of learning. Scholars gathered there to translate important books from Greek, Persian, and Indian languages into Arabic, and then they built new ideas on top of them. Among these scholars was Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician whose book on solving equations gave its name to the subject we now call algebra. His writings also helped bring the Hindu-Arabic numerals, including zero, to readers in Europe. Over time, these numerals replaced the clumsy Roman numerals, which made even simple sums slow and hard to write. Even the word algorithm, which describes a step-by-step method that computers follow, comes from a Latin form of al-Khwarizmi's name. In this way, his work still shapes how we count and calculate today.

passages.title: Food from Sunlight
passages.text: Photosynthesis is the remarkable process by which green plants convert the energy in light into chemical energy stored in sugar. Inside the leaves, tiny structures called chloroplasts contain a green pigment, chlorophyll, which absorbs mostly red and blue light while reflecting green light, and this explains the familiar color of plants. Using the absorbed energy, the plant combines carbon dioxide taken from the air with water drawn up through its roots, producing glucose and releasing oxygen as a by-product. Almost every food chain on Earth depends on this process in the end, since animals get their energy either by eating plants or by eating other animals that ate plants. In addition, plants and algae release oxygen. This is the gas that most living things need to breathe, so life as we know it could not continue without them.

options: Animals produce most of the oxygen that green plants need in order to survive.

passages.title: The Hijaz Railway
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, the Ottoman government built the Hijaz Railway to connect Damascus with Madinah. Before the railway, the same journey took about forty days by camel caravan. When the line was completed in 1908, the trip was cut to only a few days, which made the pilgrimage much safer and cheaper for travelers heading toward the holy cities. The engineers faced great difficulties along the way, including scarce water, burning heat, and shifting sand, and they built many stations, bridges, and water towers along the route. Sadly, the railway ran for barely a decade before it was badly damaged during the First World War, and it was never fully repaired. Today, the old station in Madinah has been carefully preserved as a museum, where visitors can look at original engines and learn about this bold project.

passages.title: Seeing Far and Near
passages.text: Eye doctors around the world have noticed a sharp rise in myopia, or nearsightedness, among children in recent decades. A person with myopia can see nearby objects clearly, but distant objects, such as writing on a classroom board, look blurry. Although the genes children inherit from their parents play a role, researchers have found two other factors that seem especially important. The first is spending long periods on close-up activities, such as reading or using digital devices, and the second is not spending enough time outdoors. Natural daylight appears to slow the abnormal lengthening of the eyeball that causes nearsightedness. For this reason, many specialists recommend that children spend at least two hours outside each day. They also suggest a simple rule for close work: every twenty minutes, look at something about six meters away for twenty seconds.

passages.title: Fresh Water from the Sea
passages.text: Because Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers and only limited supplies of groundwater, the kingdom depends heavily on desalination, the industrial process of removing dissolved salt from seawater to produce water that people can drink. In the past, most plants relied on thermal distillation, which involves heating seawater until it evaporates and then cooling the vapor so that it condenses as pure water; however, this method uses enormous amounts of energy. More and more modern plants now use reverse osmosis instead. In this method, powerful pumps force seawater through special membranes whose microscopic pores let water molecules pass but block the salt. Although reverse osmosis is far more efficient, it leaves behind a thick, salty liquid called brine, which must be disposed of carefully so that it does not harm sea life. Engineers are therefore testing plants powered by the sun and searching for useful ways to handle brine, hoping to make fresh water both affordable and kind to the environment.

passages.title: The Great Traveler
passages.text: In 1325, a twenty-one-year-old scholar named Ibn Battuta left his hometown of Tangier, in present-day Morocco, planning to perform the pilgrimage to Makkah. He could not have anticipated that his journey would continue, with breaks, for nearly thirty years. Over that time he covered an estimated one hundred twenty thousand kilometers by land and sea, a distance greater than that of almost any other traveler of his age. His travels carried him across North Africa, East Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Persia, Central Asia, India, Southeast Asia, and China, and in some places, such as Delhi and the Maldives, he worked as a judge. When he finally returned home, he described his memories to a writer, who turned them into a detailed book. Historians still consult this account today, because it describes the customs, governments, and trade of fourteenth-century societies that few other sources record in such careful detail.

passages.title: How Muscles Grow Stronger
passages.text: When athletes perform demanding exercises such as sprinting or lifting weights, they create microscopic tears in the fibers of their muscles. Although this damage may sound harmful, it actually starts a sophisticated repair process. During the following hours and days, the body delivers proteins and nutrients to the injured fibers and rebuilds them, so that they become slightly thicker and stronger than before. This rebuilding, however, happens mainly while the body rests rather than during training itself, which is why coaches stress the importance of good sleep and regular recovery days. Athletes who train hard without enough rest may suffer from constant tiredness, falling performance, and a higher risk of injury, a condition that is sometimes called overtraining. For this reason, well-planned training programs deliberately mix periods of intense effort with periods of rest, giving the muscles the time they need to grow.

passages.title: An Ocean Being Born
passages.text: Geologists regard the Red Sea as a remarkable natural laboratory for studying how continents split apart and how new oceans begin. About thirty million years ago, the Arabian Plate began slowly pulling away from the African Plate, stretching and cracking the crust between them until the low land in the middle was eventually flooded by seawater. This movement continues today at a rate of roughly one to two centimeters each year, and along the center of the sea, hot melted rock rising from deep inside the Earth cools and hardens into fresh ocean floor. As a result, scientists often describe the Red Sea as an embryonic ocean, one that is still at an early stage of the same process that, over a far longer period of time, produced the wide Atlantic Ocean. Researchers who study its volcanoes, its hot springs on the sea floor, and its unusually warm and salty deep pools hope that what they learn will help explain the forces that keep reshaping the surface of our planet.

passages.title: Engineers Learn from Nature
passages.text: Engineers increasingly practice biomimicry, the deliberate copying of designs from living things that have been refined through millions of years of evolution. One famous example involves Japan's high-speed trains, whose early models produced a thunderous boom whenever they emerged from tunnels, because they pushed a wall of compressed air ahead of them, and residents living nearby complained about the noise. An engineer who was also a keen birdwatcher recalled that the kingfisher dives from the air into water with hardly a splash, thanks to its long, narrow, pointed beak. When the team redesigned the front of the train to resemble that beak, the noise decreased dramatically, and the train also consumed less electricity while traveling faster than before. Similarly, researchers investigating desert beetles that collect droplets of water from morning fog have developed special surfaces capable of gathering water in dry regions. Examples like these show that living things often offer elegant, energy-saving solutions to problems that ordinary engineering methods had struggled to solve.

passages.title: How Habits Form
passages.text: Psychologists who study human behavior have found that habits develop through a repeating pattern, often described as a loop, that has three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. The cue, such as a certain time of day or a familiar place, triggers a behavior almost automatically, and the reward that follows reinforces the connection between the cue and the behavior. As this loop is repeated again and again, control of the behavior gradually shifts to parts of the brain that handle automatic actions rather than careful, deliberate decisions. Many people believe that forming a new habit takes exactly twenty-one days, but one widely cited study found that participants needed an average of sixty-six days, and the time varied greatly from person to person. Understanding this process suggests some practical strategies. People who want to build useful habits, such as reading or exercising regularly, should link them to the same cue every day and should expect that the new behavior will become truly automatic only after weeks of steady effort.
